title: Unified API or Managed API Generation? When the System Your Customers Run Has No API
summary: A unified API normalizes systems that already publish APIs into one schema. Managed API generation builds and maintains access to a system that has none. When each fits, a comparison table, how to run both behind one adapter, and a payroll example.
body_markdown:
A unified API normalizes many systems that already publish APIs into one schema, so you write one integration per software category. Managed API generation, which is what Integuru does, creates and maintains access to one specific system that has no usable API, working through the customer's own authenticated account. The first gives you breadth across a common model, and the second gives you depth on a named system.


You are rolling AI features out to thousands of customers, and the unified API you already pay for covers payroll, HR and accounting, so the first weeks go well. Then the same support ticket keeps arriving in different words: the assistant has to read and write in the restaurant POS, the reservation system or the dealer management system your customer actually runs, and none of them are in the catalogue.


At Integuru we build integrations for vertical SaaS platforms in exactly that position. If every system you need is in a unified API's catalogue, use the unified API. The rest of the post covers where its coverage ends, what managed API generation does about it, a side-by-side table, how to run both behind one abstraction layer, and payroll as a worked example.


### **What is a unified API, and when is it the right answer?**


A unified API is one API in front of many third-party systems in a software category, returning their data in a single common schema. Merge calls it "an aggregation and abstraction layer on top of multiple underlying APIs." You integrate once per category, and the vendor maintains the connector to each provider behind it.


Merge, Finch and Apideck each take a different slice of that idea, as described on their own sites in November 2026:


-


**Merge** publishes common data models per category, across areas such as HRIS, ATS, CRM, accounting, ticketing and file storage, and sells a separate product called Agent Handler for AI agents that call tools.


-


**Finch** specializes in payroll, HR and benefits. It says it reaches 250+ systems through one integration, with one schema for companies, employees, pay runs and deductions.


-


**Apideck** covers categories such as accounting, CRM and HRIS, hosts the connection screen your customers use to authorize access (it calls this Vault), and offers a Proxy API for endpoints a unified API does not yet cover.


A unified API is the right answer when four conditions hold: many providers compete in the category and your customers use different ones, most of the workload is reading data, a common data model fits what your product does with that data, and the underlying systems publish APIs the vendor can connect to. Under those conditions a new provider costs you hours or days, and writing your own connectors would spend engineering time on work a vendor has already done. Nothing in the rest of this post should talk you out of that.


### **Where does a unified API's coverage end?**


A unified API's coverage ends where the underlying system stops publishing a usable API, or where your workflow stops fitting the category's common model. A vertical platform tends to reach all four edges below, usually in the same quarter.


-


**The system has no API.** A unified API connects to APIs that systems publish. Merge's Passthrough sends requests "directly to an integration's API" using account tokens it has stored, and Apideck's Proxy API calls downstream endpoints with credentials held in Vault. Both extend your reach inside systems already in the catalogue, and neither can forward a request to an API that does not exist.


-


**The API is gated.** A system joins a catalogue when its vendor's partner program and the unified API vendor's roadmap line up, and neither follows your launch date.


-


**The workflow sits outside the common model.** A common model is the overlap between providers, which is why "mark this menu item unavailable," "move a reservation to another table" or "post a repair order" belong to a vertical and not to a category. Writes follow the same logic: Merge's documentation says it supports them "based on availability from third-party platforms," and Passthrough is restricted to its Professional and Enterprise plans.


-


**The long tail is long.** Vertical software has far more niche providers than any one catalogue is likely to list, and the catalogue grows at the pace its vendor chooses. Apideck's connector guide describes new connector development as something it can commit to based on your plan, and at the time of writing it says customers cannot yet build their own.


Finch is the clearest case of a unified API pushing past that edge. Its assisted integrations cover the long tail of HR and payroll systems outside its automated network. The employer sets up a third-party administrator user in the system and Finch manages the sync on the employer's behalf; after a one-time configuration period in which nothing can be read or written, data refreshes every 7 days and changes are written back within 2 business days. For back-office payroll work that cadence is often fine. For an assistant answering a question about something that changed this morning, it is a different problem.


### **What is managed API generation?**


Managed API generation means a provider builds, hosts and maintains an API for a system that does not offer one, then gives you documented endpoints for the workflows you asked for. Integuru does this with direct HTTP requests inside the customer's authenticated account, with no browser and no RPA, and on its Fully Managed Service typically delivers a requested integration to sandbox within a few days.


In practice it runs in three steps:


1.


**Connect.** The customer signs in to their own platform account themselves, through a browser link, so credentials never pass through your code or a terminal. From the CLI,` integuru platform create` returns that link.


2.


**Build.** You describe the workflow in plain language, for example "create a reservation." Integuru analyzes the platform's network requests and produces endpoints with request and response documentation. A CLI builder run, started with` integuru integration create` , produces a draft in roughly 10 to 20 minutes, and the Fully Managed Service takes the whole request off your team.


3.


**Run.** Your product calls a hosted HTTP endpoint with an integration ID, an account ID and the action's input. Integuru's 24/7 on-call team and authentication auto-healing repair the integration when the platform changes its login flow or endpoints.


Integuru is not a normalized schema across providers, and you should not buy it expecting one. Each integration exposes the actions you scoped for that one system, in that system's own shape, so two POS integrations will not share field names unless your own adapter makes them share. What you get in exchange is read and write access to the workflows you need on a system that no catalogue covers.


Two details matter to the engineer who has to defend this to a CTO and to counsel. Integuru works only on platforms that require a login, and every integration runs on the customer's own account with their own credentials: no logged-out scraping, no fake accounts, no reuse of one customer's credentials for another. A platform's Terms of Service can still restrict automated access, so Integuru's team reads the target platform's policy during scoping, recommends the official API or partner program wherever one covers the workflow, and raises a hard blocker before any build starts. The[trust page](https://www.integuru.com/trust) sets this out, and your own counsel should still review it.


On cost, as of November 2026: the Free plan is $0 a month for 1 platform, 1 account and 100 API calls, and Production starts at $499 a month for 1 platform, 1 account, 10,000 API calls, 24/7 on-call maintenance and auth auto-healing. The[Fully Managed Service](https://www.integuru.com/managed-service) is custom-priced, and SLAs are available on it when customers ask. The 99.9%+ figure on the site is a measured success rate on paid plans, not a contractual commitment.


### **How do the two approaches compare?**


They differ most in what they promise: a unified API promises one schema over systems that already have APIs, and managed API generation promises access to the one system that does not. The table sets out the six differences that usually decide the choice.

Systems with no API, a gated API or missing write access; vertical long tail

### **Can you use both behind one abstraction layer?**


Yes, and for a platform with customers on both horizontal and vertical systems it is the sensible default. Put one internal interface in front of every external system, route each request to whichever source covers that customer's system, and keep the rest of your product unaware of which one answered. Back to your rollout: this is how the payroll and accounting features stay on the unified API while the POS, reservation and dealer system connections run on Integuru.


1.


**Define your own action contract per workflow.** Name it for what your product does (` listOrders` ,` createReservation` ,` getPayStatements` ), with the fields your feature needs and nothing the provider happens to return.


2.


**Build a coverage router.** A small table that maps each customer's system and action to a source: the unified API where the system and action are in its catalogue, an Integuru endpoint where they are not. It is a table because it will change.


3.


**Normalize at your own edge.** For unified API calls the vendor has already done the mapping. For Integuru calls, one adapter function per integration maps the endpoint's response onto your contract, which is where the schema Integuru does not provide gets written, once, by you.


4.


**Wrap every call the same way.** One timeout, one typed error and one latency log line, so a slow or failing source looks the same to the product whichever it is.


5.


**Review the router quarterly.** When a unified API adds a system or an action, switch that row. When a partner program finally opens, do the same. The[partner API guide](https://www.integuru.com/blog/partner-api-program-stalled-vertical-saas-ai-integrations) walks through the dual-track version of this, and the[iPaaS comparison](https://www.integuru.com/blog/custom-integration-vs-ipaas) covers where workflow tools fit.


The router also answers the build-versus-buy question one row at a time instead of for the whole roadmap, which is easier to defend. The[build vs. buy framework](https://www.integuru.com/blog/build-vs-buy-integration-decision) has the cost model for the rows you would otherwise build yourself.


### **Payroll: when is a unified API enough, and when does a workflow need direct access?**


Payroll is the category where a unified API is most likely to be enough, because the data is standardized and the use cases (employee directory, pay statements, deductions) are the ones a unified payroll API was built for. Finch exists for exactly this, so start there and ask three questions before reaching for anything else.


1.


**Is the customer's payroll system in the catalogue for the product you need?** Reading a directory and writing deductions are separate products, and coverage can differ between them and between automated and assisted connections. Check the provider's own field-support reference for the specific system.


2.


**Is your action an endpoint in the common model?** Reading pay statements is. A workflow an administrator performs in the product's screens, such as approving a pay run or correcting a filing, may not be, and the only way to know is to look for the action in the reference and not assume it is there.


3.


**Does the refresh cadence match the feature?** Finch's docs put automated syncs on a 24-hour cycle and assisted ones at 7 days. A nightly benefits reconciliation tolerates that. An assistant asked "what did she get paid on Friday?" while the customer waits does not.


If all three answers are yes, use the unified API and stop. If one is no, route that system or that action through Integuru and leave the rest where it is. This keeps most of the payroll surface on the vendor built for it and sends only the specific gap to a direct integration, whether that gap is a system missing from the catalogue, an action missing from the model, or a cadence too slow for the feature.


### **FAQ**


**How does a managed integration service differ from a unified API when the target system has no public API?**


A unified API normalizes systems that already publish APIs, so it has nothing to connect to when the target has none. A managed integration service such as Integuru's Fully Managed Service builds and maintains direct HTTP access to that specific system in the customer's authenticated account, and you call it as an ordinary endpoint. The trade is no common schema across providers.


**Can Merge's Passthrough or Apideck's Proxy API reach a system with no API?**


No. Merge describes Passthrough as sending requests directly to an integration's API, and Apideck's Proxy API forwards calls to downstream endpoints using stored credentials. Both extend what you can do inside systems already connected to the unified API. A system with no API, or one missing from the catalogue, needs a different route.


**Does Integuru give me a normalized schema across providers?**


No. Each Integuru integration exposes the actions you scoped for one system, with documented request and response formats for that system. If you want one contract across several systems of the same type, you define it in your own adapter, which the abstraction layer above is designed for.


**How long does it take to add a system?**


With a unified API it is immediate when the system is already in the catalogue. With Integuru, a CLI builder run produces a draft integration in roughly 10 to 20 minutes, and the Fully Managed Service typically delivers a requested integration to sandbox within a few days. Your own testing and customer consent set the rest of the calendar.


**What does Integuru cost compared with a unified API?**


As of November 2026 Integuru's Free plan is $0 a month, Production starts at $499 a month per platform with 24/7 on-call maintenance, and the Fully Managed Service is custom-priced. Unified API pricing varies by vendor, plan and category, so compare each vendor's current pricing page against your system count.


**Is it acceptable to connect through a customer's own account?**


It depends on the platform's terms, which is why Integuru reads them during scoping and flags hard blockers before building. Every integration runs on the customer's own credentials in an authenticated session, with no logged-out access. A platform's Terms of Service can still restrict automated access, so take the specifics to your own counsel.
